concept.name: Point-in-Time Recovery

relationships.description: Connects Point-in-Time Recovery to database indexing in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Point-in-time recovery (PITR) pairs periodic physical base backups with continuous transaction log archiving (such as PostgreSQL WAL or MySQL binlogs) so you can rewind a database to any exact second, transaction ID, or log sequence number before a destructive event.
spark.keyTakeaway: Snapshots alone lose everything written since the last backup; PITR bounds data loss to your log-shipping interval by replaying committed changes up to the exact instant before corruption.

concept.whyItMatters: Logical and physical snapshots run on coarse schedules—typically every 6 to 24 hours—leaving an unacceptable data-loss window when a bad migration, `DELETE` without a `WHERE` clause, or ransomware attack hits production. PITR closes that gap to seconds or minutes by treating the database's append-only transaction log as an immutable replay stream.
whenToUse: Production OLTP databases where losing more than a few minutes of committed transactions violates RPO SLAs.
Guarding against logical corruption (accidental `DROP TABLE`, bad batch updates, application bugs) that replication faithfully copies to standbys.
Spinning up isolated forensic clones of production at a historical timestamp to debug billing discrepancies or audit state.
whenNotToUse: Ephemeral caches, session stores, or derived search indexes that can be rebuilt from a primary source of truth faster than replaying logs.
Single-table or single-row surgical rollbacks when the database is 20 TB and you have logical backups or soft-delete/temporal tables available.
Workloads with zero tolerance for RTO delays where `pg_basebackup` + WAL replay takes hours unless paired with warm standbys or copy-on-write storage snapshots.
keyPoints: PITR requires two distinct artifacts: a consistent physical base backup (e.g., `pg_basebackup`) and an unbroken chain of archived write-ahead log segments (e.g., 16 MB PostgreSQL WAL files) starting from the backup's start LSN.

Recovery is non-destructive to history only if you restore into a fresh cluster or standby and advance `recovery_target_time`, `recovery_target_xid`, or `recovery_target_lsn` up to—never past—the bad transaction.
High-write workloads generate massive WAL volume (e.g., 14 GB/hour at 4,000 TPS), making parallel WAL fetching (`pgBackRest` `process-max`) and `archive_timeout` tuning critical for both RPO and RTO.
PostgreSQL creates a new timeline ID (`00000002`, `00000003`) every time a recovered cluster is promoted, preventing new writes from overwriting the original timeline's archived WAL segments.
An untested PITR archive is indistinguishable from a broken one: a single missing or corrupted WAL segment breaks the replay chain at that LSN and halts recovery.

examples.title: Reversing an unguarded production UPDATE in PostgreSQL
examples.scenario: At 14:22:18 UTC, a deployment script runs `UPDATE invoices SET status = 'VOID'` without a `WHERE` clause on a 450 GB PostgreSQL 16 cluster. Streaming replicas apply the update within 12 ms, so failing over does not help.
examples.outcome: Using `pgBackRest`, operators restore the 02:00 UTC base backup onto a new instance, set `recovery_target_time = '2026-10-12 14:22:15 UTC'` and `recovery_target_action = 'pause'`, verify the intact `invoices` rows, promote to Timeline 2, and cut over traffic in 24 minutes with 3 seconds of lost writes.

examples.title: Forensic clone for a financial reconciliation bug
examples.scenario: Finance reports that ledger balances drifted after a nightly settlement job 3 days ago, but live tables only store current balances.
examples.outcome: An engineer restores an isolated AWS RDS Aurora PITR clone to `2026-11-09T23:59:50Z` (10 seconds before the job ran), compares account deltas against `2026-11-10T00:05:00Z`, and isolates the exact rounding bug without touching production.

tradeOffs.pro: Setting `archive_timeout = 60s` or continuous WAL streaming (`pg_receivewal`) caps data loss to under a minute even on low-traffic databases.
tradeOffs.con: Frequent forced WAL switches pad partially filled 16 MB segments, inflating S3/GCS archive storage and object-PUT API costs.

tradeOffs.pro: Daily full or differential base backups keep WAL replay windows short, bounding recovery time to minutes.
tradeOffs.con: Frequent physical backups consume disk I/O, network bandwidth, and object storage, especially when `full_page_writes = on` spikes WAL size after checkpoints.

tradeOffs.pro: Physical PITR recovers an entire multi-terabyte cluster to a sub-second boundary without table-locking or SQL parsing overhead.
tradeOffs.con: You cannot restore a single dropped table directly into the live cluster; you must restore the whole cluster (or tablespace) separately and export the table.

failureModes.name: Broken WAL chain (missing segment)
failureModes.description: A transient S3 upload error, disk-full event on `pg_wal`, or premature retention cleanup deletes a single 16 MB WAL file between the base backup and the target time.
failureModes.mitigation: Monitor `pg_stat_archiver.failed_count` and alert if `last_archived_time` lags > 5 minutes; use `pgBackRest` or `WAL-G` with checksum verification and retain at least two full base backup cycles.

failureModes.name: Overshooting the recovery target
failureModes.description: An operator guesses the incident timestamp 10 seconds too late, replays the destructive `DROP TABLE`, and promotes the cluster.
failureModes.mitigation: Always set `recovery_target_action = 'pause'` (not `'promote'`) so you can run read-only `SELECT` checks before issuing `SELECT pg_wal_replay_resume()` or promoting; keep the original timeline's WAL untouched.

failureModes.name: Timeline collision after repeated recoveries
failureModes.description: Recovering twice from the same base backup without timeline isolation causes tools or operators to mix WAL segments from Timeline 1 and Timeline 2.
failureModes.mitigation: Use timeline-aware archiving tools (`pgBackRest`, `WAL-G`) that store `.history` files and never overwrite existing WAL segments; specify `recovery_target_timeline = 'latest'` intentionally.

failureModes.name: RTO blowout from unthrottled WAL accumulation
failureModes.description: A bulk backfill generates 800 GB of WAL between weekly base backups; during an outage, single-threaded `restore_command` replays at 60 MB/s and takes nearly 4 hours.
failureModes.mitigation: Schedule daily incremental/differential backups (`pgBackRest --type=incr`), enable parallel WAL prefetch (`archive-get-queue-max`), and run monthly automated restore drills that measure actual RTO.

commonMistakes: Assuming streaming replication or Multi-AZ failover replaces PITR—replicas apply `DROP TABLE` and bad `DELETE`s in milliseconds.
Leaving `pg_basebackup` without `-X stream` or verified WAL archiving, producing an inconsistent base backup that refuses to start.
Setting `recovery_target_action = 'promote'` on the first restore attempt instead of `'pause'` to inspect the recovered state first.
Deleting old base backups aggressively without checking whether any retained WAL segments depend on them.
Never running an end-to-end restore test, only discovering years later that IAM permissions or KMS keys block `restore_command` in the recovery environment.

sections.content:
## The idea

Every ACID database already writes every state change to an append-only transaction log—Write-Ahead Log (WAL) in PostgreSQL, Redo/Binlog in MySQL—before dirty pages hit data files. Point-in-time recovery exploits that log as an out-of-band time machine.

Instead of relying solely on periodic snapshots, you pair two streams in durable object storage (such as S3 or GCS):

1. **Base backups**: A consistent physical copy of the cluster's data directory taken at time $T_0$ (recording a starting Log Sequence Number, e.g. `0/1A000060`).
2. **Continuous WAL archive**: Every 16 MB WAL segment generated after $T_0$, shipped asynchronously via `archive_command` (or `pg_receivewal`) with checksums.

To recover to any target $T_{target} > T_0$, you restore the base backup onto a clean host, configure `restore_command` to pull archived WAL segments, and instruct the engine to stop replay at the exact `recovery_target_time`, `recovery_target_lsn`, or `recovery_target_xid` just prior to the fault.

## Concrete walkthrough

Suppose a 400 GB PostgreSQL 16 cluster takes a full `pgBackRest` backup at `02:00 UTC` (start LSN `42/80000028`) and ships 16 MB WAL segments to `s3://db-backups/prod-pg/` with `archive_timeout = 300s`. At `11:14:07.412 UTC`, an operator accidentally runs `TRUNCATE TABLE user_sessions;`.

1. **Pinpoint the cutoff**: Inspect `pg_waldump` on the latest archived WAL segment or query application audit logs to confirm the `TRUNCATE` committed at `11:14:07.412 UTC` (XID `9841204`).
2. **Restore the base backup**: On a standby-sized host, run `pgbackrest --stanza=prod --delta --type=time --target="2026-11-12 11:14:05+00" --target-action=pause restore`.
3. **Replay WAL**: PostgreSQL enters recovery mode, fetches segments from `42/80000028` up to `11:14:05 UTC` (~9.2 GB of WAL at ~250 MB/s takes ~37 seconds), and pauses before applying XID `9841204`.
4. **Verify & promote**: Connect read-only, confirm `SELECT count(*) FROM user_sessions;` returns the expected 18.4M rows, then run `SELECT pg_wal_replay_resume();` (or `pg_ctl promote`), creating **Timeline 2** (`00000002.history`) and switching application DNS/PgBouncer to the recovered primary.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Targeting precision: time, XID, LSN, and restore points
sections.content:
## Targeting precision: time, XID, LSN, and restore points

Choosing the right recovery target parameter determines how cleanly you stop before a bad transaction:

- **`recovery_target_time`**: Best when you know the wall-clock timestamp from application logs or APM traces. Vulnerable to clock skew across app servers; always aim 2–5 seconds before the logged error.
- **`recovery_target_xid`**: Stops at an exact PostgreSQL transaction ID found via `pg_waldump` or `log_line_prefix` (`%x`). Combined with `recovery_target_inclusive = false`, it stops cleanly right before the offending transaction.
- **`recovery_target_lsn`**: Targets a byte offset in the WAL stream (e.g., `42/9A1200F0`). Useful when two transactions share the same millisecond.
- **`recovery_target_name`**: Stops at an explicit named marker created beforehand with `SELECT pg_create_restore_point('pre_deploy_v42');` right before risky schema migrations.

## Backup and recovery strategies compared

| Strategy | Typical RPO | Typical RTO (500 GB DB) | Protects against `DROP TABLE` | Primary operational cost |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Daily `pg_dump` (logical) | 24 hours | 45–120 min (single/parallel restore) | Yes | High CPU/I/O during dump and index rebuild |
| Daily EBS / ZFS snapshot | 24 hours | 5–15 min (volume attach) | Yes | Coarse RPO; loses up to 24h of writes |
| Streaming replica (async) | < 100 ms | 15–60 sec (failover) | No (unless `recovery_min_apply_delay` set) | Double compute cost; no history rewind |
| **PITR (`pgBackRest` / `WAL-G`)** | **1–5 min (`archive_timeout`)** | **10–30 min (base + WAL replay)** | **Yes (any second)** | **WAL storage + periodic restore drills**

## Failure modes

PITR systems rarely fail loudly during normal operation; they fail silently until an outage forces a restore.

1. **Silent archiver stall**: If `archive_command` returns non-zero (e.g., expired S3 credentials), PostgreSQL retains unarchived WAL files in `pg_wal/` until the local disk hits 100% and the database panics.
2. **Split-brain timelines**: Promoting a recovered cluster without updating `archive_command` or isolating the stanza can cause Timeline 2 to overwrite or collide with Timeline 1 metadata.
3. **Unbounded WAL replay time**: Heavy `UPDATE`/`VACUUM` bursts or `CREATE INDEX` operations can generate 50+ GB of WAL in an hour; without differential backups, replay becomes the dominant bottleneck in RTO.
4. **Missing `recovery_target_action = 'pause'`**: Defaulting to `'promote'` immediately opens the cluster to new writes, making it impossible to rewind a few seconds earlier without restarting the entire base restore.

## Production tooling and cloud-managed PITR

Self-managed PostgreSQL clusters typically use **pgBackRest** (C-based, parallel compression, page-level checksums, incremental/differential backups) or **WAL-G** (Go-based, streaming LZ4/Zstd compression to S3/GCS/Azure Blob). For MySQL 8.0, **Percona XtraBackup** provides hot physical base backups paired with continuous binary log (`binlog`) archiving replayed via `mysqlbinlog`.

Managed services automate the plumbing but still enforce hard limits: **AWS RDS / Aurora** ships transaction logs to S3 every 5 minutes (capping RPO at ~5 minutes) with a maximum retention of 35 days; **Cloud SQL** retains transaction logs for 7 days by default; **Neon** and **Aurora** separate storage from compute so PITR branches mount copy-on-write pages in seconds without copying terabytes.

## Practical checklist

- Enable `wal_level = replica` (or `logical`), `archive_mode = on`, and `archive_timeout = 300` (5 minutes) to bound RPO even during quiet traffic periods.
- Use `pg_create_restore_point('pre_migration')` before every destructive DDL or backfill script.
- Alert when `pg_stat_archiver.failed_count > 0` or `now() - last_archived_time > interval '10 minutes'`.
- Schedule daily differential backups and weekly full backups so WAL replay never exceeds 24 hours of write volume.
- Run an automated monthly PITR drill in staging that restores to a random timestamp 48 hours in the past, verifies row counts, and records actual RTO.

interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Point-in-Time Recovery. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?

commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Point In Time Recovery

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Point-in-time recovery (PITR) pairs periodic physical base backups with continuous transaction log archiving (such as PostgreSQL WAL or MySQL binlogs) so you can rewind a database to any exact second, transaction ID, or log sequence number before a destructive event.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Recovery Instance applies the primary invariant and coordinates with PgBouncer / DNS.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, PgBouncer / DNS experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Monitor `pg_stat_archiver.failed_count` and alert if `last_archived_time` lags > 5 minutes; use `pgBackRest` or `WAL-G` with checksum verification and retain at least two full base backup cycles.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Snapshots alone lose everything written since the last backup; PITR bounds data loss to your log-shipping interval by replaying committed changes up to the exact instant before corruption.
Avoid trap: Assuming streaming replication or Multi-AZ failover replaces PITR—replicas apply `DROP TABLE` and bad `DELETE`s in milliseconds.
Avoid trap: Leaving `pg_basebackup` without `-X stream` or verified WAL archiving, producing an inconsistent base backup that refuses to start.
When to reach for it: Production OLTP databases where losing more than a few minutes of committed transactions violates RPO SLAs.
When to reach for it: Guarding against logical corruption (accidental `DROP TABLE`, bad batch updates, application bugs) that replication faithfully copies to standbys.

putItTogether.title: Putting Point In Time Recovery Together
putItTogether.summary: Snapshots alone lose everything written since the last backup; PITR bounds data loss to your log-shipping interval by replaying committed changes up to the exact instant before corruption.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Point In Time Recovery before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Using `pgBackRest`, operators restore the 02:00 UTC base backup onto a new instance, set `recovery_target_time = '2026-10-12 14:22:15 UTC'` and `recovery_target_action = 'pause'`, verify the intact `invoices` rows, promote to Timeline 2, and cut over traffic in 24 minutes with 3 seconds of lost writes.
